SDK migration¶

bigdata-client and bigdata-research-tools are removed. Use REST (BIGDATA_API_KEY) / bigdata-smart-batching / OpenAI. Pass company CSVs (RP_ENTITY_ID, COMPANY_NAME) instead of watchlists. See Thematic_Screener_CLI and MIGRATION_PATTERNS.md.

Daily Digest for the Crude Oil Market¶

Why It Matters¶

In commodity markets like crude oil, timely awareness of trending news can directly influence trading strategies, hedging decisions, and market forecasts. As news cycles accelerate, being able to identify not just what is being talked about but also its potential market impact is essential for staying ahead of price-moving developments.

What It Does¶

This workflow identifies, verifies, clusters, and summarizes the most relevant and impactful news trends in the crude oil market using the Bigdata API for retrieval and large language models for topic analysis. It produces both daily market reports and structured datasets that can be used for monitoring or backtesting.

How It Works¶

The notebook implements a four-step agentic workflow built on Bigdata API:

  • Lexicon Generation of industry-specific jargon to maximize recall in news retrieval.

  • Content Retrieval via the Bigdata API, splitting searches into daily windows and parallelizing keyword lookups for speed.

  • Topic Clustering & Selection to verify, group, and summarize news into ranked trending topics, scoring each for trendiness, novelty, impact, and magnitude.

  • Custom Report Generation in the form of a daily digest with a configurable ranking system, supported by granular news sources for verification.

A Real-World Use Case¶

This cookbook illustrates the full workflow through a practical example: tracking daily stories in the crude oil market during the Israel-Iran tensions of June 2025. You'll learn how to transform unstructured news into structured, ranked insights on market-moving narratives.

Setup and Imports¶

Async Compatibility Setup¶

Run this cell first - Required for Google Colab, Jupyter Notebooks, and VS Code with Jupyter extension:

Why is this needed?¶

Interactive environments (Colab, Jupyter) already have an asyncio event loop running. When bigdata-research-tools makes async API calls (like to OpenAI), you'll get this error without nest_asyncio:

RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop

The nest_asyncio.apply() command patches this to allow nested event loops.

💡 Tip: If you're unsure which environment you're in, just run the cell below - it won't hurt in any environment!

In [1]:
import nest_asyncio
# NOTE: nest_asyncio.apply() is intentionally NOT called here. It patches the
# event loop in a way that breaks sniffio's async-library detection used by
# openai's AsyncOpenAI client (every async call fails with
# "unknown async library, or not in async context"). This notebook uses
# top-level `await` on the real async functions directly instead of the
# retired sync asyncio.run() wrappers, so nested event-loop support isn't needed.
In [2]:
import datetime
start = datetime.datetime.now()

Defining Your Daily Digest Context and Parameters¶

To perform a trending topics analysis, we need to define a few key parameters:

  • Main Theme (main_theme): The main topic, asset class, or context to analyze (e.g. Crude Oil)

  • Point of View (point_of_view): The additional instructions to the LLM-based Impact and Magnitude generation. Use this parameter to add your domain expertise and contextualize your own definition of Financial Materiality.

  • Time Period (start_date and end_date): The date range over which to run the search

  • Document Type (document_type): Specify which documents to search over (transcripts, filings, news)

  • Model Selection (llm_model): The AI model used for semantic analysis and topic classification

In [7]:
# ===== Context Definition =====
main_theme = 'Crude Oil'

point_of_view = "a crude oil trader, where price is influenced by supply-demand dynamics, geopolitical events, and market sentiment. \
As a trader, you focus on changes in production, inventories, and economic indicators from key markets."

# ===== Specify Time Range =====
# Cost-control smoke run: single-day window to minimize billed API/OpenAI usage.
start_query = '2025-12-11'
end_query = '2025-12-18'

# ===== Query Configuration =====
document_type = "news"  # was DocumentType.NEWS (SDK) -> REST document_type filter value

# ===== LLM Specification =====
llm_model = "gpt-5.6-luna"

Define Output Paths¶

We define the output paths for our results.

In [8]:
# Define output file paths for our report
output_dir = "report"
os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

export_path = f"{output_dir}/daily_digest_{main_theme.lower().replace(' ', '_')}.csv"

Instantiating the Lexicon Generator¶

In this step, we identify the specialized industry-specific jargon relevant to the crude oil market to ensure a high recall in the content retrieval.

In [9]:
# Cost control: fewer seeds than the original 5 -> fewer OpenAI calls for this smoke run
lexicongenerator = LexiconGenerator(openai_key=OPENAI_API_KEY, model="gpt-5.6-luna", seeds=[123, 123456, 123456789, 456789, 789])
In [10]:
keywords = await lexicongenerator._generate(theme=main_theme)

Content Retrieval from Bigdata Search API¶

In this section, we perform a keyword search on the news content with the Bigdata API to retrieve documents, splitting the search over daily timeframes and multi-threading the content search on the individual keywords for speed purpose. The user can define the time range below to generate daily reports between the start and end dates.

With the list of market-specific keywords parameters, you can leverage the Search functionalities in bigdata-research-tools, built with Bigdata API, to run search at scale against news documents. We need to define 2 more parameters for search:

  • Frequency (freq): The frequency of the date ranges to search over. It should at least match the frequency of your daily digest. Supported values:
    • Y: Yearly intervals.
    • M: Monthly intervals.
    • W: Weekly intervals.
    • D: Daily intervals. Defaults to D.
  • Document Limit (document_limit): The maximum number of documents to return per query to Bigdata API.
In [11]:
# ===== Query Configuration =====
document_limit = 10
frequency = 'D'  # Query frequency
In [12]:
# Full lexicon keywords (pre-migration scale).
search_keywords = keywords if keywords else [main_theme]
print(f"Searching Bigdata for: {search_keywords}")

results, daily_keyword_count = search_by_keywords(
    keywords=search_keywords,
    start_date=start_query,
    end_date=end_query,
    scope=document_type,
    freq=frequency,
    document_limit=document_limit)

print(f"Retrieved {len(results)} unique documents")
results.head()

Topic Clustering and Summarization¶

In this step, we perform topic modelling using a large language model to verify and cluster the news. Then, the summarization ensures topic selection identifying the top trending news for crude oil, while deriving advanced analytics to quantify the trendiness (based on news volume), novelty (based on daily changes in summaries), impact and magnitude (based on the financial materiality on crude oil prices) of the trending topics.

Before performing the topic clustering, we apply a verification layer to remove the news that are not relative to the oil market

In [13]:
semaphore_size = 1000 # Maximum number of concurrent requests to Openai API

# Assuming unique_reports is your DataFrame
filtered_reports = await filter_irrelevant_news(results, llm_model, OPENAI_API_KEY, main_theme, semaphore_size)

# Phase 1: Extraction
all_results, trending_topics_df, unique_reports = await phase1_extract_topics(
    unique_reports=filtered_reports,
    start_query=start_query,
    end_query=end_query,
    main_theme=main_theme,
    model=llm_model,
    api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
    batches=3
)

# Phase 2: Flattening  
flattened_df, total_cited = phase2_flatten_topics(
    trending_topics_df=trending_topics_df,
    unique_reports=unique_reports
)

# Phase 3: Consolidation
flattened_consolidated, mapping, stats = await phase3_consolidate_topics(
    flattened_raw_topics_df=flattened_df,
    model=llm_model,
    api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
    main_theme=main_theme
)

# Phase 4: Summarization
flattened_with_summaries = await phase4_summarize_topics(
    flattened_df=flattened_consolidated,
    model=llm_model,
    api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
    main_theme=main_theme,
)

# Phase 5: Generate Titles
flattened_with_titles = await phase5_generate_titles(
    flattened_df=flattened_with_summaries,
    model=llm_model,
    api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY
)

# Phase 6: Postprocessing
final_df = await phase6_postprocess(
    flattened_df=flattened_with_titles,
    api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
    main_theme=main_theme,
    total_cited_for_summary=0,
    unique_reports=unique_reports
)

Topic Scoring¶






















Trendiness and Novelty Scores: We derive analytics related to the trendiness of the topic based on the news volume, and the novelty of the topic based on the changes in daily summaries, evaluating the uniqueness and freshness of each topic.


















In [15]:






filtered_df = final_df[final_df['Volume_Score'] >= 2]
flattened_trending_topics_df = filtered_df.copy()
# Calculate trendiness and novelty scores, assessing the uniqueness and freshness of each topic
flattened_trending_topics_df = await add_advanced_novelty_scores_to_df(flattened_trending_topics_df, api_key = os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY'], main_theme = main_theme)

















































Financial Materiality: We derive analytics related to the impact (Positive, Negative) and magnitude (High, Medium, Low) of the topics, inferring their  market impact on crude oil prices. The inference is based on the price mechanisms involving supply and demand dynamics, geopolitical factors among others.


















In [16]:






flattened_trending_topics_df = add_market_impact_to_df(flattened_trending_topics_df, api_key = os.environ['OPENAI_API_KEY'], main_theme = main_theme, point_of_view = point_of_view)

























We display the results of topic modeling and summarization. The Topic column represents the themes inferred through topic clustering using a LLM, which groups the news articles based on their content and underlying themes. The Summary provides a synthesized overview of all news articles within the same topic, offering a high-level view of the key messages for each cluster. The Topic is then rephrased into a concise form based on the summary. The Text_Summary provides a detailed summary of each individualchunk, capturing its core message.






















For verification purpose, this actionable timestamped dataframe contains the granular news clustered into relevant topics, and also the advanced analytics of trendiness, novelty, impact, and magnitude scores to be potentially used for backtesting.


















In [17]:






flattened_trending_topics_df.to_csv(export_path, index=False)

























Generate a Custom Daily Digest¶






















In this step, we rank the topics, allowing the user to customize the ranking system to reindex the news, based on their trendiness, novelty, and financial materiality on crude oil prices. We finally display a daily market update, supported by the corresponding granular news and sources for verification purpose.






















The user selects the date for the report summarizing the top trending topics, and customizes the ranking system to prioritize the topics based on volume (trendiness and media attention), novelty (based on the emergence of new daily news), impact direction (positive or negative), and magnitude (financial materiality). The ranking system prioritizes the criteria in the order specified by the user, allowing for a tailored focus on the most relevant aspects of the data.






















The order in which the criteria are listed in user_selected_ranking determines their priority for ranking the topics within the report. The first criterion in the list has the highest priority, followed by the second, and then the third. The user can customize the ranking by choosing to prioritize impact direction (positive or negative), novelty, magnitude, or volume, and has the flexibility to select 1, 2, or all 3 criteria based on their specific needs.

The Day in Review


    

  • Global oversupply remains the dominant bearish driver: Forecasts point to a 2026 surplus of roughly 1.9–4.0 million bpd, with Brent near the low-$60s and WTI below $60. Contango, rising tanker inventories and growing storage underscore weak near-term balances.
    • 

  • OPEC+ paused planned Q1 2026 production increases after restoring part of its earlier cuts, offering short-term price support. However, rising non-OPEC supply and doubts about member compliance limit the impact.
    • 

  • Chinese demand and stockpiling are cushioning the surplus: January–November crude imports averaged 11.45 million bpd, while refinery throughput rose 4% year over year. Still, slowing industrial and petrochemical demand and peak-consumption concerns could weaken China’s role as the main demand buffer.
    • 

  • Venezuelan exports face significant disruption risk after U.S. seizures, tanker sanctions and a blockade order caused vessels to reverse course and raised freight and insurance costs. PDVSA could be forced to shut in extra-heavy crude if storage fills and imported diluent supplies are blocked. Chevron’s license continues to provide a stabilizing channel for some exports.
    • 

  • Russian oil flows are being disrupted and rerouted rather than removed: Ukrainian attacks, infrastructure damage and expanded Western sanctions are reducing refinery and export capacity, while Indian purchases of Urals are expected to fall from about 2 million bpd to 800,000 bpd. Cargoes are being redirected toward China, widening discounts and increasing shipping costs, but the global surplus limits the bullish price effect.
    • 

  • Potential EU legislation for a full Russian oil ban by late 2027 would intensify Russia’s need to redirect crude to Asia, increasing voyage distances, sanctions exposure and discounts while forcing Europe to secure alternative supplies.
    • 

  • U.S. crude inventory draws briefly supported WTI and Brent, with stocks around 4% below the five-year average and lower Cushing inventories. However, rising gasoline stocks, expected future builds and persistent global oversupply suggest the tightening is temporary.
    • 

  • Lower prices are beginning to curb U.S. shale investment: Falling rig counts and weaker economics could reduce 2026 output, while ExxonMobil’s aggressive Permian expansion toward 2.5 million bpd risks adding supply and deepening the near-term glut. Longer-term declines in shale investment may eventually tighten balances.
    • 

  • Additional medium-term supply is advancing: Saudi Arabia’s Jafurah gas project could free crude currently burned domestically for export; Kuwait is using artificial-lift technology to sustain mature fields; and Canadian oil-sands expansion, including Cenovus’s MEG acquisition, adds durable heavy-oil production.
    • 

  • California refinery closures create regional product risk, not a global crude shortage: Valero and Phillips 66 shutdowns could remove nearly 20% of California’s refining capacity, reducing local crude demand while increasing dependence on seaborne crude and imported refined products.
    • 

  • Sanctions are reshaping tanker and crude-trading economics: Longer voyages, shadow-fleet activity, idle Russian tankers and demand for compliant vessels are raising freight and legal costs, while owners renew aging fleets to serve changing trade routes.
    •

OPEC+ Freezes Q1 2026 Output Hikes to Head Off Looming Oil Surplus


OPEC+ has paused further planned production increases during the first quarter of 2026 after raising output by 137,000 barrels per day in December, seeking to prevent a projected supply surplus from worsening. The group is still gradually restoring the 2.2 million barrels per day of cuts introduced in early 2024, with about 1.2 million barrels per day remaining, but production at November levels could already exceed estimated 2026 demand for OPEC+ crude by roughly 60,000 barrels per day. The pause offers short-term support for oil prices and reflects concerns over expanding non-OPEC+ supply, weaker cyclical demand and the possible return of disrupted or sanctioned barrels. Its effectiveness will depend on member compliance and whether output growth elsewhere continues; Saudi Arabia’s lower official selling prices for Asia and higher exports to China could further dilute the impact of restraint. OPEC+ production policy therefore remains a key swing factor for crude markets and may require additional action if fundamentals deteriorate.

ExxonMobil’s Permian Expansion Risks Deepening Oil Glut as Output Targets 2.5 Million Barrels per Day


ExxonMobil is accelerating its Permian Basin expansion as part of a broader upstream strategy, targeting roughly 2.5 million barrels per day of total production by 2030. The increase in Permian output is expected to add to rising U.S. crude supply, potentially worsening concerns about a global oil glut and weighing on prices in the near term. Targa Resources, ExxonMobil’s largest customer, is positioned to benefit by transporting Permian crude to the Gulf Coast and export markets. Over the longer term, however, Goldman Sachs expects aging U.S. shale assets and the maturation of the shale model to slow production growth, with lower prices potentially reducing investment and supporting an eventual price recovery.

SBM Offshore Extends Angola FPSO Operations to 2032 with Brownfield Upgrades

U.S. Crackdown on Venezuelan Oil Shipments Risks Forcing PDVSA Production Cuts


U.S. enforcement against Venezuelan crude exports escalated with the seizure of the sanctioned VLCC Skipper, forfeiture proceedings against its vessel and cargo, sanctions on additional tankers and operators, and President Donald Trump’s order for a blockade of sanctioned vessels entering or leaving Venezuela. The measures have disrupted China-bound shipments, prompted tankers including Bella 1, Seeker 8, Karina and Eurovictory to reverse course, increased freight, insurance and legal risks, and encouraged the use of naval escorts and shadow-fleet tactics. Venezuelan exports, previously estimated at roughly 550,000–765,000 barrels per day and directed primarily to China, could fall sharply if enforcement expands beyond sanctioned vessels. Although the immediate volume at risk may be limited, blocked cargoes and rapidly filling storage and terminal capacity could force PDVSA to shut in production, particularly because Venezuela needs imported diluents to move its extra-heavy crude. The action has raised a geopolitical risk premium and supported Brent and WTI, but ample global supply, alternative heavy-crude sources and crude already held near China have contained the broader market impact. The central risks are wider U.S. interdiction, confrontation with Venezuela, further damage to PDVSA’s revenues and logistics, and the potential conversion of shipping disruption into a sustained production decline.

Ukrainian Strikes and Western Sanctions Squeeze Russian Oil Exports


Russian crude exports are facing simultaneous disruption from Ukrainian attacks, infrastructure outages and tightening Western sanctions. Ukrainian drone and missile strikes have hit at least 28 Russian refineries, including the Slavyansky refinery and the Nikolaevskaya depot, worsening domestic fuel shortages and reducing refining and export capacity; a separate attack forced the closure of a Baltic Sea oil terminal, while maritime-drone risks have pushed tankers leaving Novorossiysk onto longer routes through waters near Georgia and Turkey. Damage to a Caspian Pipeline Consortium mooring also temporarily disrupted a system carrying about 1.6 million barrels per day of Kazakhstan’s crude. U.S., EU and UK sanctions on Russian producers, infrastructure, tankers, traders and the shadow fleet—including new EU designations covering nearly 600 vessels—are increasing legal, logistical and shipping constraints, with Washington considering further measures if Moscow rejects a Ukraine peace proposal. Sanctions and scrutiny have sharply reduced Indian purchases of Urals crude, from roughly 2 million barrels per day in June to an expected 800,000 barrels per day in December, leaving cargoes and tankers idling near China and pushing Urals discounts wider. Russian oil-product shipments fell to about 1.7 million barrels per day in the first half of November, a more than three-year low. Although alternative routes, opaque shipping practices and rerouting may preserve some flows, floating storage, longer voyages and accumulating unsold cargoes are raising costs and uncertainty. These risks support crude prices by threatening seaborne supply, though the broader global oil surplus limits the overall price impact.

Global Oil Prices Face Prolonged Pressure as Supply Outpaces Weak Demand


Global crude prices remain under pressure as production growth is expected to outpace relatively weak demand through 2026. Forecasts from the IEA, EIA, Barclays and other analysts point to a surplus ranging from roughly 1.9 million to 4 million barrels per day, while OPEC presents a more balanced outlook. Rising output from OPEC+, the Americas and other producers, together with weaker consumption signals from China and sluggish global industrial activity, has pushed Brent toward the low-$60s and WTI below $60, with some forecasts allowing for mid-$50 prices. Contango in the Brent curve, rising tanker inventories and crude accumulating in storage indicate that supply is exceeding near-term demand. Geopolitical disruptions and low inventories may provide temporary support, but ample alternative supply has limited their price impact. Prolonged weakness could prompt producers to cut output, defer investment and reduce capacity, helping the market rebalance from 2027 onward, while OPEC+ retains the ability to respond if conditions deteriorate.

EU Moves Toward Full Russian Oil Ban to Crimp Kremlin Revenues


The European Parliament has agreed to advance legislation for a comprehensive ban on Russian oil imports, following measures to phase out Russian LNG and pipeline gas. The European Commission is expected to propose the oil legislation in early 2026, with implementation as soon as possible and no later than late 2027. The policy aims to reduce Russia’s fossil-fuel revenues and limit its ability to use energy dependence as geopolitical leverage. If enacted, Russia would need to redirect more crude to Asian and other markets, likely increasing shipping distances, sanctions exposure, discounts and logistical complexity, while forcing the EU to secure alternative suppliers.

Lower Oil Prices Trigger U.S. Shale Retreat, Threatening Future Supply


Lower crude prices are reducing U.S. drilling and discouraging new shale investment. Baker Hughes reported declines in active rigs in the Permian Basin and nationwide, with the U.S. count well below year-earlier levels, signaling tighter capital spending and slower future production growth as WTI and regional prices weaken. Sustained Brent and WTI prices in the mid-$50s to low-$60s could make some hydraulic-fracturing projects uneconomic, although longer laterals, electric fracking and AI-assisted targeting are allowing the most efficient producers to remain profitable at lower prices. Bank of America estimates that WTI averaging $57 per barrel in 2026 could reduce U.S. shale output by about 70,000 barrels per day, or 1%, while Bracewell sees Brent near $55 as insufficient for aggressive expansion. Persistently weak prices may eventually curb supply, helping stabilize prices near $70, but Saudi Arabia’s support for lower prices could prolong near-term weakness and increase its fiscal pressures. Goldman Sachs expects a possible mid-2026 low followed by recovery as demand rises, Russian supply declines and non-OPEC growth slows, meaning today’s price-driven investment cuts could ultimately help create a market deficit.

Sanctions Reroute Russian Crude From India to China, Stranding Urals Tankers


U.S. sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil are rerouting Russian crude from India toward China and other Asian markets rather than removing it from global trade. Indian private refiners—including Reliance Industries, HPCL, HPCL-Mittal Energy, and Mangalore Refinery—have reduced or halted purchases, while Indian Oil Corporation continues buying from non-sanctioned Russian suppliers. Indian imports are expected to fall to about 800,000 barrels per day in December from a June peak of 2 million bpd, even as state-owned refineries raised purchases 22% month over month in November. The resulting surplus has sent at least five tankers carrying roughly 3.4 million barrels of Urals crude to idle near Shandong, China’s independent-refining hub, where sellers are seeking buyers despite Chinese refiners’ preference for nearby, diesel-rich Russian Far Eastern grades. Sanctions-related difficulties with ownership transfers, compliant shipping, margins, and EU restrictions on fuels made from Russian crude are reshaping routes and downstream exports—including Reliance shipments to Australia—while pushing Urals discounts toward 2022 levels. The shift is creating regional dislocations and cheaper crude for willing buyers, but has not yet caused a global supply shortfall.

Canada Eyes New West Coast Bitumen Pipeline to Break 90% U.S. Oil Dependence


Canada is pursuing greater crude-export diversification as more than 90% of its oil currently goes to the United States. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s federal government and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith support examining a new bitumen pipeline to the West Coast, while public opinion favors expanding existing infrastructure first. Such a route would complement the Trans Mountain expansion, reduce transportation bottlenecks, improve access for Western Canadian heavy crude and bitumen, and connect oil-sands producers more directly with Asian buyers. China is the leading non-U.S. purchaser of Canadian crude shipped through Trans Mountain, while India is a major buyer of Canadian oil re-exported from U.S. Gulf Coast terminals; rising Asia-Pacific demand—from 35 million barrels per day in 2024 to a projected 41 million in 2050—strengthens the commercial case. Expanding oil-sands output from producers including Canadian Natural and Imperial Oil, alongside rising propane-plus and condensate production in Alberta and northeastern British Columbia, will increase demand for pipeline capacity and could widen regional price differentials if new infrastructure is delayed. The initiative reflects trade tensions and tariff-related pressure to reduce U.S. dependence, but faces environmental, emissions, Indigenous-rights, regulatory, and British Columbia taxation challenges. Overall, Pacific export capacity could strengthen Canada’s long-duration, non-OPEC crude supply position while increasing exposure to Asian markets and policy debates over decarbonization.

U.S. Crude Stock Draws Lift WTI and Brent, but Surplus Concerns Persist


U.S. crude inventory declines have provided short-term support for WTI and Brent by signaling somewhat tighter nearby physical balances. EIA data showed successive weekly draws, including a 1.8 million-barrel decline to 425.7 million barrels and a later 1.3 million-barrel decrease to 424.4 million barrels—about 4% below the five-year seasonal average—while Cushing stocks also fell. API estimates were considerably more bullish, including draws of roughly 9.2–9.3 million barrels, helping trigger price rebounds. Higher refinery inputs, increased crude exports and lower imports also supported near-term demand for domestic crude. However, the signal remains mixed: gasoline inventories rose sharply, indicating weak product demand or excess refinery output, and Macquarie expects a 2.5 million-barrel crude-stock build as Canadian imports increase, refinery runs soften and net imports rise. SPR replenishment, including recent purchases, offers incremental support, but the draws have not reversed concerns about ample global supply, weak margins and a potential 2026 surplus. Consequently, inventory declines are being treated as temporary bullish catalysts and evidence of modest near-term physical pressure, rather than proof of a sustained market tightening.
